content:
Hi,
I'm new to the theorem-proving language idea, but I would like learn about it. I've picked Lean to start with for now. I guess questions could go here or in 'general'?

I was reading this. Understood it fairly well until I hit that little table that says: "sort, Prop (Sort 0), Type (Sort 1), ...". There is a big jump there and it lost me. I'm pretty familiar with normal programming and type systems in, say, Rust, but what is "sort", "Prop", "True.intro" ?

Welcome! Normal programming languages don't have dependent types, so I don't think there are good parallels to Sort and Prop in Rust, but this is True.intro roughly:

enum True {
    intro
}

fn main() {
  let tt = True::intro;
}

Since it sounds like this is your first introduction to dependent types, these infinitely many "universes" (the numbered ones) might be confusing to start with, ignore them for now.
But consider this:

let x = u32
let y: x = 5

(this is invalid Rust but)

  1. Do you understand this snippet?
  2. If so, that's the basics of dependent types! But every value must have a type. y has type x. What would you say is the type of x? (equivalently, what is the type of u32?)
(languages usually use a different keyword instead of the first let above, such as type in Rust, or typedef in C, or using in C++)

Yes, I'm basically new to dependent types. But the basic idea makes a lot of sense to me. And your example makes perfect sense. let x: Type = u32. In a way it is more obvious than the "normal way" of having separate namespaces/worlds for values and types. It's "unified", and everything can be a "value".

Do you know Russell's Paradox? Ignore them at the beginning if you feel like Russell's Paradox is nonsense, and come back to this if you find Russell's Paradox really matter in your application. It is just a legal way in Lean to talk about Type of all smaller Types to get around the Russell's Paradox

Robert A said:

But the basic idea makes a lot of sense to me. And your example makes perfect sense.

Great! Now to slightly confuse you, I invite you to stare at this table for a few minutes:
(this is my stylized take on the table from the docs you said you were lost at)

Each arrow means "_ is of type _", for example lowercase true is of type Bool
And the gray texts in brackets are aliases, e.g. Type and Type 0 and Sort 1 are synonyms (for convenience)
I'll need to come back to this when I've read some more, and know what True, Prop, Fin, etc., are. Thank you! This language looks super cool so far. :)
